AI for Mobility · CGN 6933 · Module 2 companion

How BERT learns: pretrain on text nobody labelled, then adapt it with a few hundred labels

Last week you built a GPT. Change four things and it becomes a BERT. This page trains one on NHTSA complaint narratives, plays its two training games in front of you, and then attaches four different heads to a real bert-base-uncased, one for each kind of transportation text task. Every number on the page comes from a run you can repeat.

The problem BERT solves

An agency or a manufacturer sits on tens of thousands of free-text narratives: crash reports, 511 operator notes, work-zone logs, owner complaints. Almost none of them carry the label you need. BERT is a way to learn from all of that text first, without any labels, and then teach a specific job with the few labels you can afford.

What you already know that carries straight over

  • From Sept 10 (transfer learning): a big pretrained backbone plus a small head you train for your task. On Sept 10 the backbone read pixels. Here it reads words.
  • From last week (the GPT you can read): every line of the model. The BERT file used here, bert_from_scratch.py, reuses the GPT file's attention, block, softmax and training loop unchanged. The file's header lists the four edits line by line.
  • From discrete choice: both of BERT's training games end in a softmax and a cross-entropy. That is a multinomial logit with alternatives for a hidden word, and a binary logit for "did span B follow span A".

The data. Pretraining text: NHTSA owner-complaint narratives about driver assistance, braking, steering and lighting (the same corpus as last week's GPT), lowercased with punctuation and digits stripped. Duplicates were dropped, and so were the narratives that also appear in the labelled six-component dataset, so no fine-tuning test complaint was ever seen in pretraining, not even unlabelled. That leaves complaints for training and held out. The downstream tasks use the six-component set ( complaints, per component, split 70/15/15 by complaint).

1 · The model: three lookups in, one vector per token out

BERT reads a whole passage at once and hands back one vector per token. Before any attention happens, each token's starting vector is the sum of three table lookups. Hover or tap a token below to see its three indices. The example is a real training input built from one complaint.

The key equation

xᵢ = Etok[ wᵢ ] + Eseg[ sᵢ ] + Epos[ i ]
xᵢthe vector slot i starts with: D numbers ( in our model, 768 in bert-base)
Etok[wᵢ]row wᵢ of the token table, one row per vocabulary word (Word2Vec's table, in effect)
Eseg[sᵢ]one of two rows: "I am in span A" or "I am in span B". New in BERT.
Epos[i]one row per slot, 0 to T−1. Attention cannot tell order without it.

In words: the vector a token starts with is the sum of what it is, which span it belongs to, and where it sits. Everything after this line only mixes and reshapes these vectors.

Where the attention mask changes

This is the edit that gives BERT its B, for bidirectional. In GPT a token may read only itself and the tokens before it, because its job is to predict the next one. In BERT every real token reads every other real token. The only slots anyone is forbidden to read are [PAD] filler.

The price: BERT can no longer be trained on "predict the next word". With the whole sentence visible, the next word is already sitting in the input. Last week's leakage experiment showed what happens then: training loss collapses toward zero while the model learns nothing. BERT therefore needs different training games, and those are tabs 2 and 3.

Where the parameters live

bert-base counts from the Sept 17 BERT intro segment (bert_intro_numbers.py); our model's counts from mini_bert_numbers.py. bert-base's attention count includes the projection biases and that sublayer's LayerNorm; our file uses no attention biases, which is most of the gap in that row beyond width.

Going deeper (optional): one block, and a difference from the 2018 paper

Each block is the one you read line by line last week: x = x + attention(norm(x)), then x = x + mlp(norm(x)). Attention is the only place one token can read another. The MLP (D → 4D → D, GELU) works on each token by itself. In bert-base, attention holds 2,363,904 of each block's 7,087,872 parameters and the MLP holds 4,723,968.

The 2018 BERT normalised after each sublayer (post-norm) and added a LayerNorm right after the three embeddings are summed. Our file keeps the GPT file's pre-norm block unchanged, so the diff from last week stays at four edits. The parameter count is the same either way; pre-norm is simply more forgiving to train at small scale. Devlin et al., NAACL 2019, §3; Vaswani et al., NeurIPS 2017.

2 · Pretraining game one: hide a word, guess it from both sides

Masked language modelling (MLM). Hide some of the words, ask the model for each missing word, and adjust the weights when it guesses wrong. Nobody labels anything, because the complaint already contains its own answers. That is why this game could be played on billions of words.

Roll the masking rule on a real training input

Legend: [MASK] 80% random 10% kept 10%
of real slots chosen, measured over training batches
of chosen slots became [MASK]
became a random word
were left unchanged
words graded per training step. Last week's GPT graded .

The key equation

LMLM = − Σᵢ ∈ M log P( xᵢ | x∖M )
Mthe chosen slots, about 15% of the real words in the input
xᵢthe word that was really in slot i
x∖Meverything left visible, on both sides of the slot
P(·)a softmax over the whole vocabulary, which is a multinomial logit with one alternative per word

In words: make the true word as probable as possible, using only the words that were left showing. The model has to read the neighbours to win, and attention is the only way it can read them. So the game forces context into every vector as a side effect.

Quiz the model yourself

This is our MLM-only model (see tab 3 for why), running in your browser from its trained weights (stored as 8-bit integers). Pick a held-out complaint, then click any word to hide it. Switch the view to left side only and watch the guesses get worse: that is the value of bidirectionality.

Does reading both sides actually help? One hidden word, times

Each test hides one word in a complaint that neither this model nor last week's GPT ever trained on ( complaints sit in both models' held-out sets). Top-1 means the model's first guess was the hidden word.

Evaluation close
Baseline
Three counting rules built from the same training text: most frequent word, most frequent word after the left neighbour, most frequent word between the two neighbours. The last one wins.
The split
Complaints held out from both models, split by whole complaint, with duplicates removed before splitting. A random split by word would put the same narrative on both sides.
Ugly cases
Words outside the -word vocabulary are excluded from the test, which flatters every method equally. Complaints are often near-copies of each other, and that suits counting.
So why train a network at all? Filling one blank is the game, not the goal. A count table can fill a blank but cannot give you a vector to classify, compare or search with. The network is kept for the vectors it builds along the way. Tabs 4 and 5 test whether those vectors are worth anything.
Going deeper (optional): why 80/10/10, and what it costs

Why not always [MASK]? [MASK] never appears when you use the model. Swapping in a random word 10% of the time and leaving the true word 10% of the time means the model can never trust that a visible word is genuine, so it has to build a good vector at every position, not only at the blanks. In the paper's ablation (Table 8, bert-base) the choice barely moved fine-tuned MNLI (84.2 with 80/10/10, 84.3 with 100% [MASK]), but it mattered when the vectors were used frozen for named-entity recognition: 94.9 with 80/10/10 against 94.0 with [MASK] only.

What it costs. Only the chosen 15% are graded, so each step teaches from about words where a GPT step teaches from all . The paper reports MLM converging "slightly slower" than left-to-right for that reason (Appendix C.1). ELECTRA (Clark et al., ICLR 2020) replaced the game with detecting which tokens were swapped, a task "defined over all input tokens rather than just the small subset that was masked out".

Devlin, Chang, Lee & Toutanova, BERT, NAACL 2019, §3.1, Appendix C.

3 · Pretraining game two: did span B really follow span A?

Next-sentence prediction (NSP). Half the time, span B is the text that really followed span A in the same complaint (IsNext). Half the time it is cut from a random other complaint (NotNext). A two-way head reads only the [CLS] slot. The paper's reason: tasks such as question answering and inference are about the relationship between two passages, and MLM alone never looks at one.

The key equation

L = LMLM + λ · LNSP (the paper uses λ = 1: "the sum of the mean masked LM likelihood and the mean next sentence prediction likelihood")
LNSPbinary cross-entropy of the IsNext/NotNext head on the [CLS] vector, which is a binary logit
λhow much the second game counts. A knob you will meet again whenever one model is trained on two objectives, such as speed and flow, or detection and tracking.

What did NSP actually learn? Test it on pairs it was never trained on

This matches the literature. ALBERT (Lan et al., ICLR 2020) calls it out: "NSP conflates topic prediction and coherence prediction". Their NSP-trained model scored 90.5 on NSP but 52.0 on the swapped-order task (their Table 5), which is chance. They replaced NSP with sentence-order prediction, using exactly the swapped pairs above as the negatives.

The second game can crowd out the first

We trained the same network three ways on the same batches: MLM only, MLM + NSP with λ = 1 (the paper's sum), and MLM + NSP with λ = 0.1 (stopped at steps).

size of the MLM loss's gradient (norm), λ = 1 model, end of training
size of the NSP loss's gradient on the same batches
1.00
the clipping cap on the sum, as in the paper's code and in last week's GPT

Why: both games push on the same weights, and every step's push is clipped to a total size of 1.0. At the end of training the NSP gradient was still as large as the MLM gradient, so the easy game took a large share of every update. This is our model's result at 1.6M parameters. It is not a law about BERT, and the literature disagrees about NSP's value at full scale:

StudyWhat they comparedWhat they found
BERT, Devlin et al. 2019, Table 5bert-base with vs without NSPRemoving NSP hurt QNLI (88.4 → 84.9), MNLI (84.4 → 83.9) and SQuAD F1 (88.5 → 87.9)
RoBERTa, Liu et al. 2019, Table 2input formats with and without NSP, more data"removing the NSP loss matches or slightly improves downstream task performance"
ALBERT, Lan et al. 2020, Table 5NSP vs sentence-order predictionNSP learns topic; the order task learns coherence and transfers better
For your own models: when one network trains on two losses, weight them deliberately and plot each one separately. A combined loss curve that goes down can hide one objective doing all the work.

4 · The recipe, and what scale buys

The method is the GPT training loop with two losses added: AdamW, a warm-up then a decaying learning rate, gradient clipping, dropout. What separates the published BERT from ours is scale.

bert-base column: Devlin et al. 2019, §3.1 and Appendix A.2. Our column: the checkpoint files written by bert_from_scratch.py (the λ = 1 run; the MLM-only run is identical except for the loss).

Our pretraining run, step by step

Did our small pretraining produce vectors worth having?

Test: route a complaint to one of six NHTSA components, with 60, 300 or 2,940 labelled examples (balanced, three random draws each). Our model reads the first words, which is all its 64 slots allow ( of test complaints are longer).

Evaluation close
Baseline
TF-IDF + logistic regression on the same labelled examples, on the full text and on the same first words.
The split
The fixed 70/15/15 split by complaint. Learning rate and regularisation chosen on the validation split only; the test split was read once per run.
Ugly cases
Three seeds per point, and the seed-to-seed range is shown. At 60 labels (10 per class) it is several points wide, so small differences there mean nothing.

5 · One backbone, four ways to attach a head

The paper's Figure 4 shows that every downstream task needs only two decisions: how to pack the input and which output slots the new head reads. Everything else is the pretrained bert-base-uncased, fine-tuned end to end. Here are all four templates, each on a transportation text task.

What the four have in common. Every head is tiny next to the 109 million parameters it sits on, and in every case the model learned exactly what the labels said. The span model learned "a number next to mph" because that is what the labelling rule marked. The tagger learned the names on the list it was trained with. With fine-tuning, your labels are the specification. If you want the model to generalise past your labelling rule, the rule has to be broader than the thing you want it to learn.

6 · How much of the backbone do you let move?

There are three depths of adaptation, and each costs more than the one before.

Frozen vs fine-tuned, on the six-component task

Reused from the Word2Vec_to_BERT_Companion (complaint_finetune_numbers.py, bert-base-uncased, same split, 630 test complaints).

Read the [CLS] row. Frozen, the [CLS] vector is a poor summary () because pretraining only ever asked it about next-sentence prediction. Averaging all the token vectors does better (). After fine-tuning, [CLS] becomes a good summary because the classification loss flows through it. Frozen: average the tokens. Fine-tuned: use [CLS].
The paper's own comparison. On CoNLL-2003 named-entity recognition, fine-tuned bert-base scored 96.4 dev F1, and the best frozen recipe (concatenating the last four layers) scored 96.1 (Table 7). For entity tagging, frozen features came within a few tenths of a point. On our complaint task the gap is points. How big the gap is depends on the task, so measure it on yours.

Domain-adaptive pretraining: keep playing the game on your own text

We took bert-base-uncased and continued masked-word training on our complaint corpus for steps ( tokens, on 2 CPU cores), then measured masked-word loss on three kinds of held-out text.

Evaluation close
Baseline
The same bert-base before continued pretraining, scored on the same masked positions (fixed seed).
The split
Adaptation used only the pretraining split. The held-out complaints and the component-set narratives never entered it.
Ugly cases
The adaptation text has no punctuation or digits, and the component narratives keep both. Some of the gain on the first row is the model learning the stripped style. That is why the second row, in the original style, is the one to read. WikiText is the check for forgetting ordinary English.

The idea and the name: Gururangan et al., Don't Stop Pretraining: Adapt Language Models to Domains and Tasks, ACL 2020: "a second phase of pretraining in-domain (domain-adaptive pretraining) leads to performance gains".

7 · The same game on traffic data

Nothing in MLM or NSP is specific to words. Hide part of an input and reconstruct it from its context: that recipe works for any data where context predicts content. Transportation data is full of that.

BERT ideaLoop / radar detectorsVehicle trajectories (NGSIM, highD)Signal controller logs
Tokenone detector's speed or occupancy in one 5-min binone vehicle state (position, speed, acceleration) at one time stepone phase event (start of green, gap-out, max-out)
Positiontime of day and detector location. Your physics goes here.time step, and lane or longitudinal positioncycle and phase index
Segment A / Btwo corridors, or two time windowsthe subject vehicle vs its leadertwo approaches or two intersections
Masked-token gamereconstruct hidden detector readings (imputation)reconstruct a hidden stretch of trajectoryreconstruct a hidden phase event
Next-segment gamedoes window B follow window A? Watch the time-of-day shortcut: like topic in NSP, it gives the answer away.is this the real follower of this leader?did this cycle follow that one?
Downstream headincident detection, short-term predictioncar-following or lane-change predictiondetecting controller faults
Carry the NSP lesson over. In tab 3 the model solved "did B follow A?" by checking the topic. A traffic version will find an equally cheap shortcut if one exists: time of day, detector identity, the day of the week. Build negatives that share the shortcut (same time of day, a neighbouring detector) or the model learns only the shortcut.

Two places in this course already take this route: the masked link-state modelling assignment in Labs/ (hide a link's state and reconstruct it from the network around it), and the transformer-as-architecture companion (a transformer over detector tokens on METR-LA).

When to reach for it

Applications

DomainTask and templateData you would needClassical baseline
Road safetyCrash narrative → manner of collision or contributing factor (A: classify one text)Agency narrative fields; a few hundred to a few thousand coded reportsKeyword rules; TF-IDF + logistic regression
Agency operations (TIM)Match a new 511 or TMC note to an open incident (B: compare two texts)Operator notes with incident IDs, which gives pairs for freeTime and location match plus string similarity
ADAS and vehicle technologyFind mentions of driver-assistance features, including new brand names (D: tag every word)NHTSA complaints; a tag list that includes brand namesGazetteer (term list) lookup
Consulting daily workPull speeds, counts and dates out of past study reports (C: extract a span)Past report text with a few hundred marked answersRegular expressions; manual re-keying
Evaluation close: for any BERT project
Baseline
TF-IDF + logistic regression, or the rule your agency already uses, trained and tested on the same split. On coded agency prose it is often the winner.
The split
By report, incident or vehicle, and by time when you can. Narratives about one incident repeat each other, and a random split by sentence puts the answer in the training set.
Ugly cases
A control where the words that give the label away are removed; names and phrasings your labels never included; texts longer than 512 tokens; the rare class.

Check yourself

  1. A district has 60,000 unlabelled work-zone log entries and 400 entries coded "lane closure extended beyond permit". Rank these three plans and say what would change your ranking: (a) TF-IDF + logistic regression on the 400; (b) fine-tune bert-base on the 400; (c) domain-adaptive pretraining on the 60,000, then fine-tune on the 400.
  2. A vendor shows 97% accuracy for a model that flags ADAS-related complaints. Using tab 5, name the one control experiment you would ask for before believing that it will catch the next brand name a manufacturer invents.
  3. You want to pretrain a transformer on five years of freeway detector data with a "did window B follow window A?" task. From tab 3, what shortcut will it find first, and how would you build the negative pairs to take that shortcut away?
  4. Your 911 dispatch notes are routinely 700 to 900 wordpieces long. Which part of BERT's design is the problem, and what would you try?
